Most of the time I see track plans designed for operation they include a "run-around track" or a "wye" for moving power from one end of the train to another. The run-around track requires two turnouts (which can be expensive, cause trouble-spots, and electrical complexity). Wye's can require 3 turnouts - only compounding the problem.

That's why I was amazed at the simplicity of this operation seen on a BNSF line.

In it, the crew uses a single turn-out; and all you need is enough track off of the turnout for a locomotive to clear. It does require two locomotives though so it's probably best suited for diesel era layouts.

Here's the process:

  1. Lead unit cuts off train and follows the diverging route through the turnout.
  2. Trailing unit pulls train past turnout.
  3. Lead unit returns to the main and couples on to back of train (both engines are now have their short hoods facing the train).
  4. Train moves back past turnout.
  5. Trailing unit uncouples and followed the diverging route to clear the main.
  6. Lead unit moves train past trailing unit.
  7. Trailing unit moves back onto the main and couples to former lead unit, becoming the lead unit of a train moving in the opposite direction.

Sorry if any of you do this all the time... it seems unlikely that it's a well-known trick because otherwise I'd see it in more track plans that take up very little space. I'd imagine it has a name, please share if you know it.
